method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Conjunctivitis is the most common cause of an acute red eye.** Good analgesia helps the examination; a younger child may need procedural sedation to tell benign from serious conditions.
claims.source_text: Conjunctivitis is the most common cause of acute red eyes … Adequate analgesia will aid examination and procedural sedation may be required in the younger child to allow the clinician to differentiate benign from serious conditions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Sight-threatening features: severe eye pain, photophobia, decreased visual acuity, or a history of possible penetrating eye trauma.** These need specialist ophthalmology assessment.
claims.source_text: Key features of sight-threatening conditions are severe eye pain, photophobia, decreased visual acuity or a history of possible penetrating eye trauma; these conditions require specialist ophthalmological assessment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Uncommon but serious causes:** infectious keratitis, scleritis, uveitis, penetrating eye injury, endophthalmitis, acute angle closure glaucoma.
claims.source_text: Uncommon but serious conditions include infectious keratitis, scleritis, uveitis, Penetrating eye injury, endophthalmitis and acute angle closure glaucoma
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about systemic inflammation** (e.g. Kawasaki disease, PIMS-TS); **in a neonate, the birth history and any maternal STI.**
claims.source_text: Systemic features of inflammation (eg suggestive of Kawasaki disease, PIMS-TS) … In a neonate, consider birth history and history of maternal STI
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Be cautious diagnosing unilateral conjunctivitis.**
claims.source_text: Use caution when diagnosing unilateral conjunctivitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bacterial** (purulent discharge, not itchy, clear cornea without infiltrates): **eye toilet and chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops 4–6 times a day for 5–7 days.** Advise infection control, such as hand washing before and after touching the eyes.
claims.source_text: Bacterial Viral Allergic Presents with purulent discharge, conjunctival inflammation, not pruritic and cornea is clear with no infiltrates Treat with eye toilet, topical chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops 4–6 times per day for 5–7 days … Advise parents of infection control measures (eg washing hands before and after touching eyes)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hypersensitivity to chloramphenicol drops: stop and consult ophthalmology.**
claims.source_text: If hypersensitivity to chloramphenicol drops stop treatment and consult ophthalmology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The most common type** presents with watery discharge, burning and bilateral inflammation, often with URTI or gut symptoms. **It self-resolves over 1–3 weeks**: eye toilet, lubricants, cool compresses, infection control; **contagious until the eye stops tearing.**
claims.source_text: Most common type of conjunctivitis Presents with watery discharge, burning sensation, bilateral conjunctival inflammation and/or chemosis, and/or eyelid swelling Often associated with URTI or gastrointestinal symptoms … Self-resolving over 1–3 weeks. Symptom control with eye toilet, topical lubricants and cool compresses. Infection control measures. Contagious until eye stops tearing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspect herpes simplex if there are lid vesicles, reduced vision or photophobia:** swab for HSV PCR; aciclovir likely; seek specialist advice.
claims.source_text: Suspect herpes simplex infection if lid vesicles and/or reduced vision and/or photophobia: Swab for HSV PCR Likely to require treatment with aciclovir Seek specialist advice (ophthalmology, general paediatrics, infectious diseases)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bilateral watery discharge with itch or burning and lid swelling, especially in an atopic child:** consider oral or topical antihistamines and artificial tears.
claims.source_text: Presents with bilateral watery discharge with burning or itchy sensation and eyelid swelling, especially in an atopic child Consider treating with antihistamines (oral or topical) and artificial tears
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pathogens include staphylococcus, haemophilus, streptococcus, chlamydia, gonococcus and herpes simplex.** Consider gonococcus if there is **severe purulent discharge with conjunctival and lid oedema.**
claims.source_text: Neonatal conjunctivitis Pathogens include staphylococcus, haemophilus, streptococcus, chlamydia, gonococcus and herpes simplex … Consider gonococcal conjunctivitis if severe purulent discharge with conjunctival and lid oedema
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Swab the conjunctiva** for Gram stain, Giemsa stain and culture, plus gonococcal and chlamydia PCR if suspected.
claims.source_text: Obtain conjunctival swabs for gram stain, giemsa stain and cultures, and gonococcal and chlamydia PCR if clinical suspicion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Gonococcus, chlamydia and herpes simplex can cause invasive disease and may need a septic work-up.** Seek specialist advice.
claims.source_text: Gonococcus, chlamydia and herpes simplex can cause invasive disease and may require septic work up. Seek specialist advice (eg neonatology, infectious diseases, general paediatrics, ophthalmology)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Chlamydial conjunctivitis: oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg once daily for 3 days**, plus eye toilet.
claims.source_text: Treat chlamydial conjunctivitis with oral azithromycin 20mg/kg once daily for 3 days and eye toilet
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Gonococcal conjunctivitis: ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg stat.** Avoid ceftriaxone where possible in neonates under 41 weeks' gestation, particularly if jaundiced or receiving calcium-containing solutions.
claims.source_text: Treat gonococcal conjunctivitis with a stat dose of ceftriaxone 25-50mg/kg. Where possible, ceftriaxone should be avoided in neonates <41 weeks gestation, particularly if jaundiced or receiving calcium containing solutions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Herpes simplex infection or keratitis: septic work-up and IV aciclovir likely**; seek specialist advice.
claims.source_text: Herpes simplex infection and/or keratitis is likely to require septic work up and treatment with IV aciclovir. Seek specialist advice
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other organisms: chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops 4–6 times a day for 5–7 days.**
claims.source_text: Treat other organisms with topical chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops 4–6 times per day for 5–7 days
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Subconjunctival haemorrhage** is painless with no discharge. **Observe: an isolated one usually resolves within 1–3 weeks.** If recurrent, look for a cause such as a bleeding disorder. ⚠️ **In infants it may be a sign of non-accidental injury.**
claims.source_text: Subconjunctival haemorrhage Painless and no discharge … In infants, subconjunctival haemorrhage may be a sign of non-accidental injury … Observe. If isolated, usually resolves spontaneously within 1 – 3 weeks … If recurrent, investigate cause (eg bleeding disorder). Consider non-accidental injury
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If the posterior edge of a subconjunctival haemorrhage cannot be seen, consider an orbital or base-of-skull fracture.**
claims.source_text: If the posterior extent of the haemorrhage cannot be visualised consider an orbital or base of skull fracture
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Chemical or thermal burn: urgent, copious irrigation after local anaesthetic**; sedation or urgent GA may be needed.
claims.source_text: Chemical/thermal burns Presents with pain, watery discharge, conjunctival inflammation or pallor in more severe burns and/or corneal epithelial defect and/or corneal opacity … Requires urgent, copious irrigation, after local anaesthetic. Sedation or urgent GA may be required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Infectious keratitis** (purulent discharge, severe pain, vision loss; often contact-lens related): **contact ophthalmology urgently** and keep the contact lens for culture if possible.
claims.source_text: Infectious keratitis Presents with purulent discharge, severe pain, vision loss … Often associated with contact lens wear … Contact ophthalmology urgently Keep contact lens if possible for culture
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Endophthalmitis** (severe pain, purulent discharge, vision loss, hypopyon; after eye surgery, penetrating injury or keratitis): **contact ophthalmology urgently.** Likely IV **ceftazidime 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) 8-hourly and vancomycin 15 mg/kg (max 750 mg) 6-hourly.**
claims.source_text: Endophthalmitis Presents with severe pain, purulent discharge, vision loss, intense inflammation of conjunctiva and hypopyon … Risk factors: recent eye surgery, penetrating eye injury, keratitis … Likely to require broad spectrum IV antibiotics: ceftazidime 50mg/kg (maximum 2g) 8 hourly and vancomycin 15mg/kg (maximum 750mg) 6 hourly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Scleritis** (watery discharge, severe pain, vision loss): **contact ophthalmology urgently**; consider systemic inflammatory or autoimmune disease.
claims.source_text: Scleritis presents with watery discharge, severe pain, vision loss and intense inflammation of sclera, episcleral and conjunctiva … Contact ophthalmology (urgent for scleritis) Consider systemic inflammatory disease/autoimmune disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Iritis/uveitis:** pain, photophobia, blepharospasm, tearing; the pupil may be small, irregular and poorly reactive. **Contact ophthalmology.**
claims.source_text: Iritis/Uveitis Inflammation of the iris (iritis), ciliary body (cyclitis), or choroid (choroiditis) Presents with pain, photophobia, blepharospasm and lacrimation Pupil may be small, irregular and poorly reactive … Causes are autoimmune, infection, and trauma Contact ophthalmology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute angle closure glaucoma:** severe pain, cloudy vision and cornea, fixed, mildly dilated pupil, sometimes headache and vomiting. **Contact ophthalmology urgently.**
claims.source_text: Acute angle closure glaucoma Presents with severe eye pain, watery discharge, decreased visual acuity (cloudy vision), cloudy cornea and fixed mildly dilated pupil May also have associated headache and vomiting (from raised pressure) Contact ophthalmology urgently
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Involve the paediatric team** for suspected child abuse, suspected STI-related conjunctivitis, or possible systemic illness.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Any child with suspected child abuse, suspected STI-related conjunctivitis, or possible systemic illness
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider transfer** for a sight-threatening condition or management beyond the local team.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when A child with a sight threatening condition and/or management is beyond the capacity of the local team
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** sight-threatening conditions are excluded **and** treatment is started or referral made **and** follow-up or clear early-review advice is in place.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when Sight-threatening conditions have been excluded AND Appropriate treatment has been initiated as per diagnosis or referral made AND Planned follow up, or clear instructions regarding when early review is indicated has been provided to the child and family
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute red eye' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_red_eye/, retrieved 2026-09-23
